parts.title: How much electricity will Africa produce up to 2030, and how much water and carbon dioxide will that take?
parts.abstract:
Abstract

More people in Africa need electricity, so the continent has to produce more of it. To make good decisions, people need information about power plants: where they are, how much electricity they make, how much water they use and how much carbon dioxide (CO2) they release. That information should be reliable, easy to find, of high quality, free for anyone to use, and detailed enough to show where each plant is.

In this paper we present a detailed map-based record of Africa's power plants from 2020 until 2030. It covers plants that are already running, plants being built and plants that are planned. We built it by carefully searching through many public sources of information, and it includes 3,139 individual plants.

Our record forecasts that Africa's electricity production will grow by 57%, reaching 1,787,858 gigawatt-hours (a gigawatt-hour is a very large amount of electricity) from 2023 to 2030. The water used and the CO2 released rise a great deal too. This shows trade-offs between different fuels: some use a lot of water but release little CO2, and others the other way round.

Africa is stepping up in planning and building extra power plants, and the share of electricity from renewable energy is growing from 19% to 34%. However, the growth in hydropower (electricity made from moving water, for example in dams) puts more pressure on the water that is available. The power plants now being built fall slightly short of what countries have promised in their nationally determined contributions, the climate plans each country has submitted under the Paris Agreement.

Subject terms: Hydrology (the study of water on Earth), Water resources
parts.introduction_first: Today, 57% of the people in Africa have access to electricity, which is among the lowest share in the world, and it varies a lot from one country to another. The Sustainable Development Goals are a set of targets that the world's countries agreed on to make life better for everyone. Goal 7 is about clean and affordable energy, and its target 7.1 aims to make sure that by 2030 everyone can get affordable, reliable and modern energy. One way of checking progress is a measure called indicator 7.1.1, which tracks the share of people who have access to electricity. It shows that Africa is falling behind other continents.
parts.introduction_rest:
Africa is developing fast, though, and the continent is producing and using more and more electricity. There are big differences between regions, however. Only three countries, South Africa, Egypt and Algeria, produce 60% of all the electricity made in Africa. In general, countries with a larger gross domestic product (GDP), which is the total value of everything a country produces, also produce more electricity. That is why producing more electricity, and giving more people access to it, are high priorities for African governments and investors.

African countries need to plan new power plants so that they can cope with water shortages, and they need to keep CO2 emissions in mind. The power system is one important part of a wider "nexus" approach. A nexus approach looks at how different areas, such as energy, water, food, health and climate, are linked, where they help each other, and where gaining in one means losing in another. These trade-offs are the main reason we study power plants: the water they use and the CO2 they release are two important pressures on the environment, and they often pull in opposite directions.

The word "nexus" is used in different ways. It depends on which areas are included, such as energy, nature and wildlife, water, food, health or climate. In this paper we look at a few parts of the energy–water–climate nexus. We study how much water power plants use and how much CO2 they release, because these two pressures are important trade-offs.

To make well-informed decisions, people need good information about power plants: reliable, easy to find, of high quality, free for anyone to use, and detailed enough to show where each plant is. That information should include how much water each plant uses and how much CO2 it releases. Right now, such information is missing across much of Africa, both for today and for the future. Some data do exist, but they cannot give a picture of the whole continent that covers existing, building and planned power plants together with their water use and CO2 emissions.

Several databases of power plants in Africa already exist. These include the World Resource Institute's Global Power Plant Database, a database of renewable power plants in Africa, a database from the European Commission for the year 2016, and a database by Gerbens-Leenes and colleagues for the year 2020. The first two have far fewer entries for Africa than ours (Supplementary Table 1), and they do not include water use or CO2 emissions. The Global Power Plant Database only covers existing power plants, while the renewable database also includes some future renewable power plants. The last two databases do include water use, but not CO2 emissions, and they leave out future power plants.

Other researchers have worked out where power plants release CO2. For example, Guevara and colleagues made a worldwide catalogue of CO2 emissions from thermal power plants (plants that burn fuel such as coal, oil or gas) for the year 2018. However, none of these studies is detailed enough for Africa and for the year 2030 that we look at. Computer models have shown that, worldwide, the water used for energy is increasing, and they point to the places where this might happen. But these studies usually give results for whole countries. They do not show detail within a country or a river basin, and they do not take into account which power plants are actually being planned or built. The same is true for CO2 emissions.

In this paper, we study how electricity production across Africa will change, in fine detail, up to 2030. That is the target year of the Sustainable Development Goals. First, we list all the power plants that were running from 2021 to 2023. This builds on a recent study by Gerbens-Leenes and colleagues. Next, we find the power plants that will be running up to 2030, using public information about plants that have been shut down, plants that are planned and plants that are expected to be built. We add these plants, with details such as where they are, the year they start running, what fuel they burn and other details, to our record of power plants, which we call INVENTORY. INVENTORY is the main result of this paper. It includes 3,139 individual power plants and is the most detailed and up-to-date database of power plants covering Africa up to 2030 that anyone can find.

INVENTORY is not the result of a computer model. It is the result of a lot of careful, time-consuming searching through free public sources of information. We used only free sources, so that we could share our database freely too. We used GEM wiki and Wikipedia, because they give recent information on power plants, especially the large ones. We also used Power Technology, a website about the world's energy industry that gives the installed capacity (the maximum power a plant can produce) and the year a plant was put into use. In addition, we used OpenStreetMap, reports from national governments and international organisations such as the World Bank, scientific papers, company websites, reports and newspapers, which tell us when particular plants open or close. We checked and corrected the map position of every power plant using Google Maps. Supplementary Tables 2–7 list the sources we used for each power plant.

INVENTORY gives a realistic picture of the power plants that exist today and an estimate of the plants being built. We can do this because planning and building a power plant takes time, and the period up to 2030 is fairly short. According to Sovacool and colleagues, nuclear power plants and larger hydropower dams take the longest to build, on average 7 and 10 years. Small run-of-river power plants, which use the flow of a river without a large dam, take less time. Thermal power plants that burn fossil fuels take almost 5 years on average. Solar projects and wind farms take the least time, about two years and one year on average. These averages vary quite a lot, though. Our period up to 2030 is only about five years, but we are confident that we include almost all the power plants that are planned or being built, because we only include plants that are being built now or are being planned, and all of them are meant to start running by 2030 at the latest.

We also look at five other forecasts up to 2030. Four of them are based on how much electricity countries have produced in the past, and one is based on the electricity mix in the countries' climate plans (their nationally determined contributions), following Article 4, paragraph 12 of the Paris Agreement. The electricity mix means the share of electricity that comes from each kind of power plant. So we study six forecasts in total. The first is INVENTORY, and the second is the climate-plan forecast, which we call NDC. The other four forecasts take the past trends in each country's electricity production, from 1990 to 2015, as reported by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), and extend them to 2030 using our INVENTORY database up to 2023. Each of these four uses a different way of extending the trend. The first, called REGR_LIN, fits a straight line through the past values. The second, called REGR_POL, fits a smooth curve. The third, called REGR_MVAR, also takes into account how many people live in each country and its GDP. The fourth, called ARIMA, is a statistical method that predicts future values from the pattern of the recent past.

Fresh water is limited. When different parts of society, including energy, use it, many places around the world run short. Water use is growing because of economic development, more people, more people moving to cities and other factors. Africa has the fastest population growth between now and 2050, so it stands out as a key region where the demand for water is expected to rise.

Water is an important limit on how much electricity can be produced. Thermal power plants use water to cool their equipment or to keep dust down, hydropower needs water to turn its turbines, and solar panels need water to be cleaned. Different kinds of energy use very different amounts of water for each unit of electricity they make. In Africa, on average, hydropower from reservoirs uses the most water, fossil fuels are in the middle, and wind and solar power use the least. So it is important to know how much water a country will need to make electricity in the future when new power plants are planned and built.

In this study, we therefore look at two measures of water for the 2030 forecasts. The first is blue water withdrawal: the amount of fresh water taken from rivers, lakes, wetlands and underground water stores (aquifers) for any human activity. The second is water consumption: the part of that water that is not put back into the place it came from, or that evaporates into the air.

Making electricity also affects the climate, because it releases CO2, especially when fossil fuels are burned. Between 2010 and 2021, the electricity produced in Africa doubled, but Africa's share of the world's CO2 emissions stayed small, at about 3%. The Paris Agreement, signed in 2015, aims to keep global warming below two degrees compared with the time before industry began. Countries that signed the agreement work towards the goals set out in their climate plans. In Africa, 53 countries have submitted climate plans. Together, these plans aim to cut 550 million tonnes of CO2 by 2030, which is 40% of Africa's emissions today. To meet the agreement, countries need to write a national plan for how they will reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. These plans often set goals for the electricity mix, and they describe how much renewable energy they want in terms of installed capacity (in megawatts, or MW), not in terms of how much electricity is produced.

Twelve African countries, which together produce more than 40% of Africa's emissions, have also announced goals to reach net-zero emissions, meaning they will no longer add to the total amount of CO2 in the air. Many African climate plans include targets that depend on money from developed countries, amounting to 1,200 billion US dollars up to 2030. That is more than the 100 billion US dollars a year that developed countries have promised to give all developing countries from 2023. For these reasons, we also look at the CO2 emissions for the 2030 forecasts.

We share our INVENTORY in more detail than anyone has done before, with the water use and CO2 emissions of each power plant. In general, information on how much water each part of the economy uses, including electricity, is very scarce for African countries. For many countries, there is not even information for the country as a whole. A lasting lack of reliable water data is a common problem for managing water in poorer countries around the world. To manage water well and to judge where water is scarce, we need detailed information about where different users, such as electricity, take their water.

We also share all our data freely, so that anyone can use them. This matters for researchers and others working in Africa, who often do not have the money to buy good data and studies. Some companies keep databases of existing power plants. However, their data cannot be used or copied freely, and they are not shared under a Creative Commons licence, a type of licence that lets people reuse data. This holds back research on making electricity production sustainable, and it limits a discussion based on science among the people who make decisions.

The rest of this paper is organised as follows. The "Results" section gives our forecasts of electricity production, water use and CO2 emissions up to 2030. The "Discussion" section first discusses the results in general, then what they mean for policy and what we recommend, and then briefly discusses the limits and uncertainties of our work. The "Methods" section explains how we did our work, step by step, in different subsections.

In this study, we give six forecasts for 2030 for the whole of Africa on electricity production, with the water use and CO2 emissions that go with them. Our main assessment is INVENTORY, a detailed database of existing power plants and an estimate of the power plants being built and planned. We also make four forecasts based on past electricity production, to see whether Africa is stepping up in building new power plants. Finally, we make a forecast based on the climate plans, to see whether the power plants now being built, as shown in INVENTORY, match the promises countries have made.
parts.results:
## Results

### How much electricity Africa will produce up to 2030

Our map-based record of Africa's power plants (which we call INVENTORY) shows that the continent's total electricity production grew from 1,046,061 gigawatt-hours in 2020 to 1,080,938 gigawatt-hours in 2021. That is 3% more than in 2020. It then rose to 1,119,233 gigawatt-hours in 2022, which is 7% more than in 2021, and to 1,139,289 gigawatt-hours in 2023, which is 9% more than in 2022 (Fig. 1).

We forecast that INVENTORY will reach 1,787,858 gigawatt-hours in 2030. That is 741,797 gigawatt-hours more than in 2020, or 71% more than in 2020. It is also 648,569 gigawatt-hours more than in 2023, or 57% more than in 2023.

We also made five other forecasts, each based on a different way of extending past trends into the future. Four of them use regression, a method that finds the line or curve that best matches past values. The fifth, called ARIMA, uses the pattern of recent changes to predict the next ones. When we extend past electricity production from 1990 up to 2023 in these ways, they give lower amounts for 2030: 1,157,485 gigawatt-hours for the first regression forecast (REGR_LIN), 1,155,210 for the second (REGR_MVAR), 1,280,169 for ARIMA, and up to 1,414,231 for the third regression forecast (REGR_POL).

Compared with these past trends, Africa is stepping up in planning and building extra power plants to make more electricity during 2024–2030. Even so, the power plants now being built still fall short of what countries have promised in their climate plans (their nationally determined contributions). Those plans add up to 1,868,433 gigawatt-hours. Extra power plants will need to be built up to 2030 to meet these promises.

**Fig. 1**

Electricity production in Africa (in gigawatt-hours per year) from 1990 to 2015 (past years), for INVENTORY (from 2020 to 2023 and for 2030), and for the five other forecasts in 2030 (REGR_LIN, REGR_MVAR, REGR_POLY, ARIMA, NDC).

The figure shows the total, and also the amount for each type of power plant, grouped by fuel. We left out Ascension Island, Comoros, Mayotte, Reunion, St. Helena, Swaziland and Tristan da Cunha, because they do not have their own climate plans.

INVENTORY and the climate plans also differ in how much electricity each type of power plant makes in 2030 (Fig. 1). In INVENTORY, the total of 1,787,858 gigawatt-hours is split as follows: 1,098,120 gigawatt-hours (61%) from fossil fuels, 599,220 gigawatt-hours (34%) from renewable energy and 90,519 gigawatt-hours (5%) from other sources. In the climate plans, the total of 1,868,433 gigawatt-hours is split as 1,068,020 gigawatt-hours (57%) from fossil fuels, 709,352 gigawatt-hours (38%) from renewable energy and 91,061 gigawatt-hours (5%) from other sources. So the climate plans make more electricity from renewable energy, both as a share of the total and in actual amount.

The fuels differ too. INVENTORY makes much more electricity from coal than the climate plans do (331,593 compared with 269,647 gigawatt-hours). For natural gas it is the other way round (693,476 compared with 725,323 gigawatt-hours). Among the renewables, INVENTORY makes much more hydropower than the climate plans (517,501 compared with 378,598 gigawatt-hours). For solar power it is the other way round (24,570 compared with 179,645 gigawatt-hours), and the same is true for wind (30,685 compared with 109,627 gigawatt-hours).

In INVENTORY, 605 more power plants start working between 2021 and 2030 than in 2020. Together they make 742,170 gigawatt-hours, bringing the total running in 2030 to 1,792,844 gigawatt-hours (Fig. 2b). For 551 of these plants we know the exact position on the map, given as map coordinates (x and y). These 551 plants make 691,228 gigawatt-hours, bringing the total running in 2030 to 1,741,903 gigawatt-hours (Fig. 2b).

The extra power plants have been built, or are being built, and they are spread unevenly across Africa (Fig. 2a). For a large share of them, we know the year in which they actually start working. For many, we only know that they start working sometime between 2024 and 2030, because the exact year is missing.

**Fig. 2**

Total electricity production (in gigawatt-hours per year) of all power plants in INVENTORY, for each year from 2020 up to 2030 (including Ascension Island, Comoros, Mayotte, Reunion, St. Helena, Swaziland and Tristan da Cunha).

a Map of power plants whose position is known. The size of each circle shows how much electricity the plant makes, and its colour shows the year it starts working (blue means 2024–2030, but the exact year is uncertain). b Total electricity production by the year each plant starts working, for all power plants (1,792,844 gigawatt-hours, more than the 1,787,858 gigawatt-hours shown earlier because the islands are included) and for power plants whose position is known (1,741,903 gigawatt-hours). c Electricity production in each country, by the year each plant starts working, for the eleven countries with the highest amounts during 2021–2030. We made the map in a with the mapping program ArcGIS, using country and continent borders from GADM, a free database of world borders.

Which countries add the most electricity from new plants during 2021–2030? The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) adds the most, 195,891 gigawatt-hours, followed by Nigeria (92,175 gigawatt-hours) and Egypt (76,601 gigawatt-hours) (Figs. 2c and 3b).

In the DRC, most of the new plants are hydropower plants (195,823 gigawatt-hours in total), starting to work between 2024 and 2030. These are the Grand Inga Power Station (152,321 gigawatt-hours) and the Inga III Power Station (40,075 gigawatt-hours), on the lower part of the Congo river. This is the largest dam project in the world (Fig. 3a and b).

Nigeria invests in nuclear power by building the Geregu and Itu nuclear power plants (17,636 gigawatt-hours each). It is also building coal-fired plants (the Itobe project, 14,155 gigawatt-hours) and natural-gas-fired plants (for example the Sparkle Power Plant, 8848 gigawatt-hours), as well as hydropower plants (for example Mambilla, 11,777 gigawatt-hours). Its solar and waste-heat projects add up to 1159 and 1939 gigawatt-hours. In Egypt, the focus is on building a nuclear power plant (the Dabaa power plant, 35,272 gigawatt-hours) and more gas-fired power plants (together 37,410 gigawatt-hours).

**Fig. 3**

Total electricity production (in gigawatt-hours per year) of all power plants in INVENTORY, for each year from 2021 up to 2030, grouped by type of power plant (by fuel).

a Map of existing power plants (triangle, 2021–2023) and new power plants (circle, 2024–2030) whose position is known. The colour shows the type of power plant, and the size shows how much electricity it makes. b Electricity production in each country, by type of power plant, for the eleven countries with the highest amounts during 2021–2030. We made the map in a with ArcGIS, using country and continent borders from GADM.

During 2021–2030, Ethiopia increases its electricity production by 47,247 gigawatt-hours. Of this, 37,482 gigawatt-hours come from extending hydropower, 8434 gigawatt-hours from geothermal power (heat from inside the Earth), 748 gigawatt-hours from solar and 582 gigawatt-hours from wind (Figs. 2 and 3).

South Africa adds 39,283 gigawatt-hours. During 2021–2023, this includes extending a coal-fired plant by 13,810 gigawatt-hours (such as the Kusile plant of 9227 gigawatt-hours in 2022), as well as extending wind and solar power by 1656 and 256 gigawatt-hours. From 2024 to 2030, it expands gas power plants by 20,884 gigawatt-hours, such as the Coega power plant in the Eastern Cape (8017 gigawatt-hours) in 2025. It also expands solar power by 2508 gigawatt-hours, such as the Coega Solar PV Park (2221 gigawatt-hours).

Other countries that add a lot of electricity during 2021–2030 include Mozambique (33,231 gigawatt-hours in total, of which 19,171 from hydropower and 13,918 from natural gas), Algeria (31,026 gigawatt-hours, of which 30,859 from natural gas) and Zimbabwe (23,184 gigawatt-hours, of which 14,302 from extending coal-fired power plants and 7318 from hydropower) (Fig. 3). For Libya, Angola and South Sudan, the amounts are 23,129, 20,807 and 19,534 gigawatt-hours, mostly from extending hydropower and natural gas.

For the whole of Africa, INVENTORY forecasts that electricity production in 2030 will be 71% higher than in 2020. For some countries the rise is larger than this, and for others it is smaller (Fig. 4).

Countries with a large rise include South Sudan (+7443%), the DRC (+2941%), Namibia (+1905%), Sierra Leone (+371%), Zimbabwe (+328%), Madagascar (+253%), Ethiopia (+247%), Nigeria (+220%), Central African Republic (+213%), Malawi (+210%), Niger (+198%), Guinea (+196%) and Angola (+96%), along with many others.

Countries with a smaller rise than the average include large countries such as Sudan (+66%), Kenya (+66%), Libya (+43%), Algeria (+31%), Morocco (+27%), Egypt (+27%), South Africa (+13%) and Tunisia (+10%). Some of these countries, such as Egypt, South Africa, Algeria and Libya, add a lot of electricity in actual amount (Figs. 2 and 3), yet their rise is smaller than average. Some of them already have more people with access to electricity, especially in northern Africa and South Africa (Fig. 4b), and this could partly explain the smaller rise. But it is not only the general population that needs electricity. Other sectors, such as industry, mining and transport, also need it, and many of them are growing and would need more electricity.

**Fig. 4**

Key national figures on electricity production and access to electricity.

a Percentage increase in each country's electricity production in INVENTORY in 2030 compared with 2020. The average for the African continent is 71%. b Share of people in each country with access to electricity, in percent, for 2020–2022 (Sustainable Development Goal indicator 7.1.1). We made the maps in a and b with ArcGIS, using country and continent borders from GADM.

In some countries, almost no extra power plants are planned or built. Somalia, for example, adds only 6% more electricity, even though only 6% of its people currently have access to electricity. In others, INVENTORY shows no extra power plants for 2030, so the rise is 0%. These include Eritrea, where 12% of the people have access to electricity, and Guinea-Bissau, where 29% do. Because their governments and institutions are unstable, no money is being invested in building power plants to give more people access to electricity.

### How much water power plants will use up to 2030

Across Africa, INVENTORY shows that the water taken from rivers and lakes for power plants (called water withdrawal) grew from 33,097 million cubic metres in 2020 to 34,357 million cubic metres in 2021, 36,071 million cubic metres in 2022 and 38,255 million cubic metres in 2023. That is 16% more than in 2020 (Fig. 5b).

In 2023, fossil fuels account for 29% of all the water taken, and natural gas in particular takes a lot (9462 million cubic metres, or 25% of the total). Renewables account for the other 71%. Hydropower uses the most water of all, taking 27,165 million cubic metres, or 71% of the total.

**Fig. 5**

Total water withdrawal (WW) of all power plants in INVENTORY and in the climate plans (nationally determined contributions), from 2020 up to 2023 and for 2030, grouped by type of power plant (by fuel).

a Map of existing power plants (triangle, 2020–2023) and new power plants (circle, 2024–2030) whose position is known, for INVENTORY. The colour shows the type of power plant, and the size shows how much water it takes, in cubic metres per year. b Total water withdrawal (million cubic metres per year) by type of power plant for INVENTORY in 2020–2023 and 2030, and for the climate plans in 2030. We made the map in a with ArcGIS, using country and continent borders from GADM.

For INVENTORY, we forecast that water withdrawal will rise a lot, to 66,234 million cubic metres in 2030. That is 100% more than in 2020 and 73% more than in 2023. If countries meet their climate plans, water withdrawal would rise to 68,323 million cubic metres in 2030, which is 106% more than in 2020 and 79% more than in 2023.

These rises come mostly from extending natural gas and hydropower up to 2030 (Fig. 5b). Extending hydropower in particular adds a great deal of water use. Hydropower's water use goes from 27,165 million cubic metres in 2023 to 54,469 million cubic metres in 2030 in INVENTORY, and to 56,546 million cubic metres in 2030 in the climate plans.

In INVENTORY, we forecast large rises in hydropower water use up to 2030 in countries such as the DRC, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Mozambique, Zambia, Cameroon, Ghana, Tanzania and Kenya (Fig. 5a). We also forecast large rises in natural-gas water use up to 2030 in countries such as Egypt, South Africa, Nigeria, Algeria, Libya and Tanzania. In the climate plans, we forecast large rises in hydropower water use up to 2030 in countries such as Ethiopia, Nigeria, Mozambique, Zambia, Cameroon, Ghana, Tanzania and South Africa. As in INVENTORY, we forecast large rises in natural-gas water use up to 2030 in countries such as Egypt, South Africa, Nigeria, Algeria, Libya and Tanzania.

Taking more water to make electricity puts more pressure on the renewable water in Africa's main river basins (Fig. 6). A river basin is the whole area of land that drains into one river. By renewable water, we mean the water that nature keeps refilling, minus the environmental flows. Environmental flows are the water that must stay in a river to keep its plants and animals healthy. Here we use the high level of protection for environmental flows defined by Richter and colleagues.

For many river basins, the share of water taken compared with the water available grows from 2020 and 2023 to our forecast for 2030. In the Volta basin, this share grows from 42.7% in 2020 and 2023 to 49.7% in 2030. In the Zambezi basin, it grows from 8% in 2020 to 10.1% in 2023 to 14.5% in 2030. In the Nile basin, it grows from 4.8% in 2020 to 5.8% in 2023 to 6.5% in 2030. In the Niger basin, it grows from 2.8% in 2020 to 2.9% in 2023 to 6.8% in 2030. In the Congo basin, it grows from 0.1% in 2020 and 2023 to 3.4% in 2030. This will make it harder for other sectors, including nature itself, to get the water they need.

**Fig. 6**

Water withdrawal (WW) as a percentage of the renewable water available in major African river basins.

The figure highlights the basins with the highest amounts, for INVENTORY in 2020 (a), 2023 (b) and 2030 (c). For 2030, only new power plants whose position is known are included. d shows the amounts for selected river basins (top bar 2020, middle bar 2023, bottom bar 2030). We made the maps in a and b with ArcGIS, using country and continent borders from GADM.

If we use a lower level of protection for environmental flows, the share of water taken compared with the water available becomes smaller. Even so, it still grows from 2020 and 2023 to our forecast for 2030 (Supplementary Fig. 2).

### How much CO2 power plants will release up to 2030

Across Africa, INVENTORY shows that CO2 emissions grew from 641 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent in 2020 to 654 million tonnes in 2021, 671 million tonnes in 2022 and 678 million tonnes in 2023. That is 6% more than in 2020 (Fig. 7b). CO2 equivalent is a way of counting different greenhouse gases as if they were all CO2, so that they can be added together.

In 2023, fossil fuels account for 99.5% of all CO2 emissions. Of the total, oil releases 50 million tonnes (7.5%), coal releases 326 million tonnes (48%) and natural gas releases 298 million tonnes (44%). Renewables account for the remaining 0.5%.

**Fig. 7**

Total CO2 emissions (CO2e) of all power plants in INVENTORY and in the climate plans (nationally determined contributions), from 2020 up to 2023 and for 2030, grouped by type of power plant (by fuel).

a Map of existing power plants (triangle, 2020–2023) and new power plants (circle, 2024–2030) whose position is known, for INVENTORY. The colour shows the type of power plant, and the size shows how much CO2 it releases, in tonnes of CO2 equivalent per year. b Total CO2 emissions (million tonnes of CO2 equivalent per year) by type of power plant for INVENTORY in 2020–2023 and 2030, and for the climate plans in 2030. We made the map with ArcGIS, using country and continent borders from GADM.

CO2 emissions are forecast to rise up to 2030 both in INVENTORY, which is based on what is actually planned and built, and in the climate plans, which are based on policy goals. The overall rise is smaller in the climate plans than in INVENTORY.

If countries meet their climate plans, CO2 emissions would rise to 766 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent in 2030. That is 20% more than in 2020 and 13% more than in 2023. In the climate plans, emissions from oil rise to 61 million tonnes, the same as in INVENTORY. Emissions from natural gas rise to 394 million tonnes, which is 32% more than in 2023, while emissions from coal fall to 293 million tonnes, which is 10% less than in 2023.

In INVENTORY, emissions rise to 808 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent in 2030, which is 26% more than in 2020 and 19% more than in 2023. These fairly large rises come from extending fossil fuels. In INVENTORY, emissions from oil rise to 61 million tonnes, which is 23% more than in 2023. Emissions from coal rise to 364 million tonnes, which is 12% more than in 2023, and emissions from natural gas rise to 375 million tonnes, which is 26% more than in 2023.

So, for natural gas, emissions rise more in the climate plans than in INVENTORY, because natural gas is extended overall. For coal, emissions fall in the climate plans compared with INVENTORY, because coal-fired power production shrinks overall. In INVENTORY, some extra coal-fired power plants are built up to 2030, while in the climate plans, some coal-fired power plants are shut down.

In INVENTORY, we forecast large rises in coal emissions up to 2030 in countries such as Nigeria, Zimbabwe and Botswana (Fig. 7a). We also forecast large rises in natural-gas emissions up to 2030 in countries such as South Africa, Egypt, Mozambique, Nigeria, Algeria, Libya, Namibia, Côte d'Ivoire and Tanzania. In the climate plans, coal and natural gas emissions rise in the same countries. In South Africa, however, some coal-fired power plants are taken out of use (Grootvlei, Kelvin, Majumba, Matla, Sasol one and Tutuka, together 71 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent), and one natural-gas power plant is added (19 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent), compared with INVENTORY.
parts.discussion:
## Discussion

In this paper we show that Africa is stepping up in planning and building extra power plants up to 2030, so that more people can get electricity. To show this, we made the most detailed map-based record of Africa's power plants from 2020 until 2030 that anyone has so far. Our record covers 3,139 individual plants. For each one it gives the fuel (oil, coal, natural gas, hydropower, wind, sun, biomass, geothermal, nuclear and waste heat), the location (its map coordinates), the installed capacity (how much power the plant can produce, in megawatts, or MW), the electricity it produces (in megawatt-hours, or MWh), how much water it takes in and how much it uses up, its CO2 emissions, and other details such as the climate, how the plant is run and where the information came from. This level of detail, including forecasts of the future, goes well beyond existing map-based records, such as the Global Power Plant Database from the World Resources Institute (WRI), RePP Africa, the work of Gonzalez Sanchez and colleagues, and the work of Gerbens-Leenes and colleagues (Supplementary Table 1).

We forecast that electricity production will rise from 1,139,289 gigawatt-hours in 2023 to 1,787,858 gigawatt-hours in 2030, which is 57% more than in 2023. We call this forecast INVENTORY, because it is based on our map-based record. It is higher than what we would expect if electricity production simply carried on following its past trends from 1990 to 2015. We tested four ways of extending those past trends into the future, called REGR_LIN, REGR_MVAR, ARIMA and REGR_POL. This confirms that Africa is stepping up, with some countries driving the forecast and others lagging behind.

The power plants now being built (INVENTORY) fall slightly short of what countries have promised in their climate plans (the nationally determined contributions). Those plans add up to 1,868,433 gigawatt-hours. The two also differ in how much electricity each type of power plant produces in 2030. In the climate plans, renewable energy produces more electricity, both as a share of the total and in actual amount. Among the fossil fuels, INVENTORY produces much more electricity from coal than the climate plans do, while for natural gas it is the other way round. Among the renewables, INVENTORY produces more from hydropower than the climate plans, but less from solar and wind.

In 2023, making electricity took 38,255 million cubic metres of water and released 678 million tonnes of CO2-equivalent. CO2-equivalent is a way of counting all greenhouse gases together, as if they were all CO2. We forecast that both of these pressures on the environment will grow a great deal up to 2030. In INVENTORY, water use rises to 66,234 million cubic metres and CO2-equivalent to 808 million tonnes. In the climate plans, the amounts are 68,323 million cubic metres and 766 million tonnes.

Today and in our forecast, most of the water is used by hydropower, because on average it takes 105 cubic metres of water for every megawatt-hour it makes (Fig. 8). Natural gas comes next, with an average of 14.3 cubic metres per megawatt-hour. In 2023, gas made 25% of all the water used for electricity and hydropower made 71%. In 2030, gas's share falls to 15%, and hydropower's share rises to 82–83% (INVENTORY and the climate plans).

Different fuels also differ a lot in how much carbon they release for each megawatt-hour of electricity. Fossil fuels release much more than renewables, so they make up most of the CO2-equivalent today and in our forecast (Fig. 8). Coal releases an average of 1,098 kilograms of CO2 per megawatt-hour, oil 840 and natural gas 541. These amounts are very high compared with hydropower, which releases an average of just 0.8 kilograms of CO2 per megawatt-hour. In 2023, oil made 7.5% of all the CO2 released by making electricity, coal 48%, gas 44% and renewables 0.5%. In 2030, all the fossil fuels together make 98–99% of it, and hydropower less than 0.5%.

Fig. 8

Average water use and CO2 released for each fuel used in power plants in Africa. Water use is measured in cubic metres of water per megawatt-hour, and CO2 in kilograms of CO2 per megawatt-hour.

These are averages over all power plants, and single plants vary a lot. Each fuel has the same colour in the bar charts for water use (left) and CO2 (right).

These trade-offs show up in the gap between INVENTORY, which is what is actually being built and is likely to be running by 2030, and the climate plans, which is what countries have promised. INVENTORY releases more CO2-equivalent because extra fossil fuel power plants, especially coal and gas plants, are being built. In the climate plans, by contrast, several coal plants are shut down and replaced by gas plants, which release less carbon. On the other hand, hydropower that releases little carbon has been built in different parts of Africa and is still being built, and this leads to much higher forecasts of total water use for 2030. This puts more pressure on the water available in many of Africa's major river basins (Fig. 6).

Hydropower is one of the main reasons why the variety of life in fresh water is declining. Almost one in three freshwater species is threatened with extinction, and this share is always higher than for species that live on land. Hydropower is also at risk from droughts and floods, which climate change makes worse. In 2024, a drought across Southern Africa left Zambia with power cuts every day, because the reservoir of the Kariba hydropower dam did not have enough water. We forecast that the Zambezi basin, where Kariba is, will face more pressure on its water by 2030 (Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 2).

The large growth in hydropower in Africa up to 2030 is good for keeping CO2 low, but it is easily harmed by drought and might harm the variety of life in fresh water. That life includes fish and amphibians, but also large animals such as crocodiles and hippos. It matters for local people's food supply and for income from tourists who come to see wildlife.

To make electricity production more resilient, meaning better able to cope with shocks, we need a mix of different energy sources, including renewables. That mix should include not only hydropower but also solar and wind energy. Our forecast also shows solar and wind growing a lot by 2030, but hydropower still leads the growth, as it did in the past. In the past, solar and wind technology was not as good as it is now and was expensive to build, while hydropower was already a well-established technology. Wind and solar use little water and release little carbon, and they are also cheap. So building more of them can be seen as a win-win in many African settings, especially because Africa is still falling short of its climate plans by 2030.

Carlino and colleagues show that falling costs for solar and wind, together with climate change, reduce the need to build more hydropower in Africa. According to Peters and colleagues, the cost of solar panels has fallen by 90% since 2009 and the cost of wind turbines by 55–60% since 2010. This means solar and wind could lead Africa towards a sustainable mix of renewable energy in the years ahead. Across Africa, wind and solar are used far less than hydropower.

Hydropower plants take much longer to build than solar projects and wind farms: larger hydropower plants take about 10 years, while solar and wind projects take 1–2 years. So INVENTORY most probably underestimates how much new solar and wind capacity is being built up to 2030. Because Africa is more and more committed to development that releases little carbon, building more solar and wind up to 2030 might even help many African countries reach their climate plans, as long as the money is guaranteed. If more capacity is built, that would only strengthen our statement that, overall, Africa is stepping up in planning and building extra power plants. Even so, individual countries still need to step up seriously in building renewable power plants.

Policies for the electricity system therefore need to take into account how much carbon each energy source releases and how much water it uses (Fig. 8), as well as how much water is available locally (Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 2) and how much water other sectors need. This calls for nexus thinking, which means looking at energy, water and food together, because they are linked. It also calls for different government ministries (such as those for energy, environment, water, agriculture and irrigation, among others) and other groups with a stake in these decisions to coordinate and work together, so that policies on energy, water, agriculture, industry and the environment line up with each other.

For example, Kenya's Ministry of Energy and Petroleum has published the "Energy Transition & Investment Plan 2023–2050", which sets out how the country will reach net-zero emissions by 2050. Net-zero means that no more greenhouse gases are released than are removed. The plan aims to cut carbon from the energy system by building more renewables (geothermal, hydropower, solar and wind) and by making the system flexible (with batteries and with demand response, where people use less electricity when it is needed). The plan recognises that reaching net-zero in the energy sector needs a well-run way of making decisions, a good process and an action plan. These must be open and transparent, with coordination across the ministries, and the policies of each sector must fit with the country's goals.

The plan does not directly mention how much water the energy system needs or how this relates to local water. However, Kanda and colleagues confirm that Kenya's water policies should play a central part in policies that link water, energy and food. We forecast (INVENTORY) that Kenya's electricity production will rise from 12,006 gigawatt-hours in 2020 to 19,880 gigawatt-hours in 2030, which is 66% more than in 2020. This leads to a 51% rise in the water needed, from 275 to 416 million cubic metres, and hydropower makes up the largest part of this rise. Kenya already faces water stress, meaning it does not have enough water to meet its needs. Forecasts like ours should therefore be central to a broader, joined-up approach and to making policy.

We can sum up our policy recommendations as follows. First, policies for the electricity system need nexus thinking. They need to take into account how much carbon each energy source releases and how much water it uses (Fig. 8), as well as how much water is available locally and how much water other sectors need. Hydropower is at risk from more frequent and more severe droughts caused by climate change, so a mix of energy sources is needed. Building more of the cheap energy sources, solar and wind, is a win-win in many African settings. Stepping up these sources further until 2030 and beyond may help reach the climate plans.

Second, different ministries and other groups need to coordinate and work together, so that policies on energy, water, agriculture, industry and the environment line up. Third, it is essential that African countries secure the money for their planned and under-construction power plants, so that these are not delayed or cancelled. The money can come from a mix of public and private sources: private companies, international organisations such as the World Bank or the African Development Bank, development agencies of single countries, or others.

Fourth, joined-up solutions are needed. These include building a mix of different energy sources, including renewables; battery storage; a reliable national grid that also shares electricity across borders (international power pools); and small-scale solutions close to where the electricity is used. Fifth, policies need to deal with cooperation and river management across borders.

Sixth, policies should be based on data and science. Our INVENTORY is a freely available record that shows exactly where each power plant is, for the years 2020–2030. It is fundamental for building a joined-up, sustainable mix of renewable energy. Countries need to share high-quality data, including data about their power plants and how much water each sector uses.

There are many different ways and frameworks for modelling and forecasting how much electricity is supplied and how much is needed, and many review papers have been published on this. The information they start from includes social and economic drivers (such as GDP, which is the value of everything a country produces, population and market trends), the effects of energy and climate policies, the effects of sudden shocks from outside, and how the people involved take part. On the last point, there is growing interest in, and demand for, energy modellers to bring more varied views of possible and preferred futures into their models. McGookin and colleagues, for example, offer a framework that gives modellers several ways to include the views of the people involved, either throughout the process or at particular stages. Our assessment involves these people indirectly, because we use each country's own climate plan, which the country itself has developed.

We do not use advanced modelling in this paper. The main result of this paper is our map-based record of Africa's power plants (INVENTORY). It shows the real-world situation of Africa's main power plants, because power plants take a long time to build and our forecast only covers a short period up to 2030. We are confident that no model so far has modelled this situation. So INVENTORY can serve as a tool to tune existing or future models, or as a result that such models can aim for. By improving the input data and settings of existing or future models, INVENTORY offers a real-world forecast up to 2030 for training or fine-tuning models at the level of Africa, of single countries or of parts of countries.

We also use three regression models (REGR_LIN, REGR_POL and REGR_MVAR) and ARIMA. A regression model finds the pattern that best links past values to later ones, and ARIMA is a method that predicts future values from the recent past. These methods support our statement that Africa is stepping up in planning and building extra power plants. We use simple regression models to forecast electricity production over the short period 2024–2030 because of the specific aim of our analysis: to compare electricity production in INVENTORY with past trends, not to build highly accurate or finely tuned forecasts with models. In this way, we place real government plans, including power plants now being built, within the history of past electricity production. Those plans are already shaped by cost, policy, technical choices and the involvement of private companies. Simple regression models like ours are well suited to this purpose. They let us check whether planned and under-construction power plants match, go beyond or fall short of past patterns.

Like any study that forecasts the future, our analysis has some limitations and uncertainties, which we discuss below.

The INVENTORY forecast assumes that all planned and under-construction power plants will be finished by 2030. We made this assumption because the time left until 2030 is fairly short and because of the average time it takes to plan and build power plants. On the one hand, this assumption may miss some delays, cancellations or changes in energy policy. However, it is impossible to foresee such events, or certain shocks (such as conflict, a natural disaster or a financial shock) that could cause them. On the other hand, extra power plants that take a fairly short time to plan and build (cheap options such as solar power plants and wind farms) could be built up to 2030, and we have no information about these at the moment.

We also made a version of INVENTORY in which solar power plants and wind farms take 1 year to become operational, all other power plants take 2 years, and nuclear and large hydropower plants may be delayed. This lowers the forecast electricity production for 2030 from 1,787,858 gigawatt-hours to 1,504,848 gigawatt-hours. Much of this drop comes from assuming that the large hydropower plants on the Congo River are delayed: the Grand Inga Power Station (152,321 gigawatt-hours) and Inga III (40,075 gigawatt-hours). Other large hydropower plants include the Mambilla power plant in Nigeria (11,777 gigawatt-hours) and Mphanda Nkuwa in Mozambique (10,710 gigawatt-hours). We also assume that the two new Nigerian nuclear power plants (17,636 gigawatt-hours) are delayed.

This delayed version of INVENTORY therefore adds up to only 1,504,848 gigawatt-hours, which is 16% less than 1,787,858 gigawatt-hours. That is still more than the highest of the past-trend forecasts (REGR_POL for 2030, 1,414,231 gigawatt-hours, Fig. 1). Delaying only these hydropower plants lowers the total by 14%, and delaying only these nuclear power plants lowers it by 4%. So even with all these delays, we can confirm that Africa is stepping up in electricity production. Because INVENTORY most probably underestimates solar power plant and wind farm projects in the later years up to 2030, our statement that Africa is stepping up remains valid.

INVENTORY should therefore be seen as an estimate, based on the information available today.

We first submitted this paper in November 2024, so we present our analysis up to the year 2023 as existing data and all later years (2024–2030) as forecasts. In 2026, we were able to use real-world data to identify the extra power plants that became operational in 2024 and 2025. We compare the results in Supplementary Table 8. For total electricity produced, INVENTORY gives 1,222 gigawatt-hours for 2024 and 1,251 gigawatt-hours for 2025, while the real-world data give 1,161 and 1,220 gigawatt-hours. That is a difference of 5% for 2024 and 2% for 2025. These are fairly small differences. They are generally caused by power plants becoming operational later than expected, or by new power plants becoming operational, which INVENTORY does not capture. This is especially true for power plants that take a short time to build, such as solar and wind, as we explained earlier. The same is true for the number of power plants, where the differences are 0% and −1% (Supplementary Table 8).

The regression forecasting methods (REGR_LIN, REGR_POL and REGR_MVAR) and ARIMA are based on past trends, which may not match what happens in the future, especially when the energy landscape is changing fast. We used these methods only to see how well they forecast the amounts given by INVENTORY by 2030. All three regressions and ARIMA forecast less total electricity for Africa than INVENTORY shows for 2030 (Fig. 1), which supports our statement that "Africa is stepping up in planning and building extra power plants". This statement holds for Africa as a whole, while results for single countries and single fuels can differ.

Supplementary Fig. 3 shows that, for electricity made from natural gas in Egypt, ARIMA gives the best forecast of the INVENTORY amount for 2030 (290,810 gigawatt-hours). REGR_LIN (Eq. (3)) and REGR_MVAR (Eq. (5)) give 247,599 and 256,742 gigawatt-hours, which is less than INVENTORY. REGR_POL (Eq. (4)) gives 332,388 gigawatt-hours, which is more than INVENTORY.

For several fuels in different countries, REGR_POL forecasts a value close to the INVENTORY amount for 2030, while REGR_LIN, REGR_MVAR and ARIMA forecast less than INVENTORY (Supplementary Fig. 4). One example is electricity made from gas in Libya (Supplementary Fig. 4a), where REGR_POL forecasts 64,856 gigawatt-hours and INVENTORY 67,591 gigawatt-hours, while REGR_MVAR forecasts 39,965 gigawatt-hours, REGR_LIN 40,796 gigawatt-hours and ARIMA 47,820 gigawatt-hours. Other examples are solar panels in South Africa (REGR_POL 7,107 gigawatt-hours and INVENTORY 5,673 gigawatt-hours, Supplementary Fig. 4b), natural gas in Tanzania (REGR_POL 9,155 gigawatt-hours and INVENTORY 8,346 gigawatt-hours, Supplementary Fig. 4c) and solar panels in Namibia (REGR_POL 711 gigawatt-hours and INVENTORY 608 gigawatt-hours, Supplementary Fig. 4d). This clearly shows that using REGR_POL is justified for our short-term forecasts.

In many cases, even REGR_POL forecasts less electricity for 2030 than INVENTORY (Supplementary Fig. 5). This is the case for electricity made from gas in Nigeria, where REGR_POL forecasts 49,610 gigawatt-hours but INVENTORY gives 53,618 gigawatt-hours, which is much higher (Supplementary Fig. 5a). Other examples are solar panels in Kenya (REGR_POL 651 gigawatt-hours and INVENTORY 994 gigawatt-hours, Supplementary Fig. 5b) and hydropower in Ethiopia (REGR_POL 39,936 gigawatt-hours and INVENTORY 55,759 gigawatt-hours, Supplementary Fig. 5c). For geothermal in Tanzania, the regression forecasts 0 gigawatt-hours for 2030, because no geothermal power had been built there until 2023. The new geothermal investment, which INVENTORY captures with 1,349, is therefore missed by the regression forecasts and by ARIMA. Examples like these show why the different regression methods, and ARIMA, forecast less electricity in total than INVENTORY shows for 2030 (Fig. 1).

Our study does not include possible improvements in how efficiently power plants work, or new technologies that might appear by 2030. These could change both the estimates of electricity production and the water use and CO2 emissions that come with it. When new thermal power plants (plants that burn fuel to make steam) are built, they might work more efficiently. However, because our forecast covers only a short period (2024–2030), we assume that efficiency does not change much. Also, power plants last a long time, and only a small share of them are new thermal plants, so differences between countries will also be small. Most of the growth in electricity production comes from renewables such as hydropower, solar and wind.
parts.methods:
## Methods

In this study we look at how much electricity Africa produces from 2020 to 2030, and at the water and carbon dioxide (CO2) that come with it. We look at three things: water withdrawal, which is the water a plant takes in; water consumption, which is the water it uses up and cannot return to the river or sea; and CO2 emissions. Our work builds partly on a recent study by Gerbens-Leenes and colleagues (reference 11). They made the most detailed map-based record of Africa's electricity production and the water it needs for the year 2020, including 2,534 individual power plants, each with its exact location.

We carried out our study in five steps.

In Step 1, we updated the 2020 record year by year up to 2023. In Step 2, we made a forecast of how much electricity each country will produce in 2030 for our map-based record, which we call INVENTORY. This forecast uses what we found about plants that have been shut down, plants that are planned, and plants that are being built in each country.

In Step 3, we made four more forecasts of electricity production in 2030. They are based on how each country's electricity production changed from 1990 to 2019, according to two international energy agencies, the International Energy Agency (IEA, reference 1) and the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA, reference 22). We also used the 2020 record and its 2023 update. To stretch these past trends forward to 2030, we used three different regression methods. A regression is a way of finding the line or curve that best matches a set of data points. The first is a straight line (REGR_LIN). The second is a curve that can bend once (REGR_POL). The third uses two extra pieces of information about each country, its population and its GDP (the total value of everything a country produces), to help predict electricity (REGR_MVAR). We also made a forecast with a method called ARIMA (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average), which we explain below.

In Step 4, we made a fifth forecast for each country, called NDC. It is based on what each country's national policies say it will do, as set out in its nationally determined contributions under the Paris Agreement (reference 21).

Finally, in Step 5, we worked out water withdrawal, water consumption and CO2 emissions for each type of power plant, using INVENTORY and the three regression forecasts for 2030. We describe all five steps below, and Supplementary Fig. 1 shows them as a picture. Table 1 gives an overview of the different forecasts, and Table 2 lists where our data came from.

Table 1

The six different forecasts

| Forecast | What it is |
|---|---|
| INVENTORY | A map-based record of Africa's power plants from 2020 until 2030. We built it by carefully searching through many free public sources of information, which took a lot of time. It is not the result of a computer model. It gives a realistic picture of the power plants that exist and an estimate of the ones being built. |
| Regressions and ARIMA | Forecasts for 2030 made by stretching past trends forward, using three different regressions. These regressions are based on how each country's electricity production changed from 1990 to 2019, according to the IEA (reference 1) and IRENA (reference 23), and on the 2020 record and its 2023 update. |
| REGR_LIN | A straight-line regression |
| REGR_POL | A regression with a curve that can bend once |
| REGR_MVAR | A regression that also uses population and GDP |
| ARIMA | Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average |
| NDC | Each country's forecast of its electricity, based on its national policies as set out in its nationally determined contributions under the Paris Agreement |

Table 2

Where our data came from

| Data | Source |
|---|---|
| Electricity production for each type of power plant, for each year in our study, and for the NDC | Supplementary Table 2 |
| Power plants and their features in 2020 | Gerbens-Leenes et al. (reference 11) |
| Sources we used to find the power plants that started working between 2021 and 2023, for each country | Supplementary Table 3 |
| Sources we used to find the power plants for 2024–2030, for each country | Supplementary Table 4 |
| How much water each type of power plant takes in (water withdrawal) | Supplementary Table 5 |
| How much water each type of power plant uses up (water consumption) | Supplementary Table 6 |
| How much CO2 each type of power plant releases | Supplementary Table 7 |
| Natural renewable water, mapped in fine detail (0.1 degrees, or 11.1 km at the equator) | Vanham et al. (reference 65) |

### Step one: Building the 2023 record

To build the 2023 record, we followed the method described by Gerbens-Leenes and colleagues (reference 11). We used free public sources of information to find new power plants, and for each one we noted its fuel, its installed capacity (how much electricity it can produce at most), how much electricity it makes, whether it uses fresh water or salty water, and where it is. Because the sources are free to use, we can share our finished record freely too.

We used GEM wiki (reference 17) and Wikipedia (reference 18), because they give recent information on power plants, especially the large ones. We also used Power Technology (reference 19), which gives the installed capacity and the year each plant started working. In addition, we used OpenStreetMap, reports from national governments or international organisations such as the World Bank, scientific papers, companies' websites, reports and newspapers. These told us when particular plants opened or closed.

We looked at satellite images to check the location of every power plant. For all thermal power plants (plants that make electricity by heating water, for example by burning fuel), we also used the images to find out how they cool their water. Some use a cooling tower, some take in water, use it once and let it out (once-through cooling), and some cool without any water (dry cooling). The images also showed whether the plants use fresh water or salty water.

As an example, we first worked out the installed capacity in 2023 for each country c, fuel f and technology t, which we call IC2023,c,f,t (in megawatts, MW). We used Eq. (1):

(1) IC2023,c,f,t = IC2020,c,f,t + ICnew,c,f,t − ICold,c,f,t

Here, IC2020,c,f,t is the installed capacity in 2020 for country c, fuel f and technology t. ICnew,c,f,t is the capacity of new plants added between 2020 and 2023, and ICold,c,f,t is the capacity of plants that were shut down during those years.

Next, we estimated how much electricity country c, fuel f and technology t made in 2023, E2023,c,f,t (in megawatt-hours, MWh), using Eq. (2):

(2) E2023,c,f,t = IC2023,c,f,t × SE2023,c,f,t

Here, SE2023,c,f,t is the specific electricity generation: how many megawatt-hours each megawatt of installed capacity makes (MWh per MW). We took these figures from Gerbens-Leenes and colleagues (reference 11). We added the new power plants to their record, noting the year each one first started working (2021, 2022 or 2023).

### Step 2: Forecasting electricity production in 2030 for INVENTORY

In Step 2, we estimated how much electricity each country will produce in 2030 for INVENTORY. First, we estimated how much installed capacity the power plants that are running will have in 2030. To do this, we searched free public sources of information about how electricity production is set to grow in every African country. We included in INVENTORY every power plant that is being built now or is planned to start working by 2030. Then we used Eq. (1) for the years 2020 to 2030. After that, we used Eq. (2) to get electricity production for each country, assuming that the specific electricity generation (how much electricity each megawatt of capacity makes) stays the same over this period.

### Step 3: Forecasting electricity production in 2030 with regression

In Step 3, we estimated electricity production in 2030 for each country using four forecasts: REGR_LIN, REGR_POL, REGR_MVAR and ARIMA.

We estimated electricity production in 2030 from how fast it grew between 1990 and 2020, using regression. First, we gathered electricity production for each country for every year from 1990 to 2020. The IEA (reference 1) gives these data for the largest African countries over that period, but some smaller countries were missing. For those, we used data from IRENA (reference 22), which often covers a shorter period. These countries are Burkina Faso, Gambia, Guinea, Liberia, Mali, Mauretania, Mauritius, Niger, Reunion, Seychelles, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Sudan and Togo. For Ascension Island, Chad, Djibouti, Equatorial Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Lesotho, Malawi, Mayotte, St Helena, Swaziland, Tristan da Cunha, Western Sahara and Zimbabwe, we had no past data. For these, we used our own estimates for 2020 and 2023 from the 2020 record (reference 11) and the 2023 record (Step 1).

Using these past trends, we estimated electricity production for country c, fuel f and technology in 2030 with a straight line (REGR_LIN), EL2030,c,f,t (MWh), as in Eq. (3):

(3) EL2030,c,f,t = a × YEAR + b

Here, a is the slope of the line, which shows how much electricity production changes for each extra year. We worked it out from the link between the year (the input) and electricity production (the result). The letter b is the intercept: the value of electricity production when the year is zero.

We did the same thing with a curve that can bend once, called a second-order polynomial regression (REGR_POL), EP2030,c,f,t (MWh), as in Eq. (4):

(4) EP2030,c,f,t = c × YEAR² + d × YEAR + e

Here, c, d and e are fixed numbers. We found them by trial and improvement (iteration), adjusting them until the total of the squared gaps between the curve and the data points was as small as possible.

We used a curve that can bend once, and not a curve that bends more. For many countries, a curve that bends once matches the data points very well all the way up to 2030, which is a short time to forecast. In African countries, electricity production generally does not meet demand by 2030, so there is no need for the curve to flatten out, as a third-order polynomial regression could do.

We also used a regression that takes two factors into account at once (REGR_MVAR), EMV2030,c,f,t (MWh). It uses each country's population and GDP over the same years for which we have electricity data, as in Eq. (5):

(5) EMV2030,c,f,t = r × GDP + s × Population + t

Here, r is the fixed number that shows how much GDP adds to electricity production, and s is the fixed number that shows how much population adds. The letter t is the intercept of the curve. We found all three by trial and improvement, again making the total of the squared gaps as small as possible.

#### How we used ARIMA

We also forecast electricity production from 2023 to 2030 with the ARIMA model, written ARIMA(p,d,q). Many articles have used it to forecast both energy production and energy demand, for example Luzia and colleagues (reference 60), Prakash and colleagues (reference 61) and Suo and colleagues (reference 62). The model is shown in Eq. (6):

(6) (1 − Σ(i=1 to p) ϕi B^i)(1 − B^d) y_t = (1 − Σ(j=1 to q) θj B^j) η_t

Here, y_t is the value we observed at time t. B is the backshift operator, a mathematical tool that lets the model refer to earlier values. η_t is the white noise, the random ups and downs that the model cannot predict. ϕ and θ are the numbers the model estimates. We estimated them with a method called likelihood optimisation, which finds the values that make the data we actually saw most likely, using the statsmodels library for the Python programming language (reference 63).

The ARIMA model has three parts. The autoregressive part, AR(p), uses earlier values to predict the next one. The differencing part, of order d, looks at the change from one year to the next instead of the values themselves. The moving average part, MA(q), uses the random ups and downs of recent years. So the first step is to decide what values of p, d and q to use.

For each set of data, we did the following. (1) We checked whether the data were stationary, meaning their average and spread stay roughly the same over time, to decide d. For this we used two tests: (a) the augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) test, which starts from the assumption that the data are not stationary, and (b) the KPSS test, which starts from the assumption that they are. (2) To decide p and q, we looked at (a) the autocorrelation function (ACF), which shows how strongly each year's value is linked to earlier years, to identify MA(q), and (b) the partial autocorrelation function (PACF), which shows the same links after removing the effect of the years in between, to identify AR(p).

For every country and technology, the data after differencing showed the same pattern. (1) The ADF test failed while the KPSS test passed after differencing once, which confirmed d = 1. (2) The ACF showed a strong spike at lag 1 (the link between one year and the year before) that faded quickly, which suggests q = 1. (3) The PACF also showed a strong spike at lag 1 that faded quickly, which suggests p = 1.

So we used the standard model ARIMA(1,1,1) for every dataset, so that all the results could be compared fairly. To fit it, we used the fit ARIMA function in the statsmodels Python library (reference 64).

To fit ARIMA for each type of power plant, we used an automated script that processes many datasets in a row. This made sure that every dataset, whatever its country, technology or file format, was handled in exactly the same way, so the work can be repeated. We include the script with this paper, as described in the section "Code availability".

Finally, we checked the data and looked for errors with several quality-control steps, both before and after fitting the model. (1) We put all datasets on the same time scale, using the start of each year (YS) as the time stamp, so that the years were evenly spaced. (2) We checked how many data points each dataset had, and left out those with fewer than 10 valid values, because ARIMA becomes unreliable with fewer points. (3) We checked whether the ARIMA fitting had failed. (4) We looked at AIC values, a score that weighs how well a model fits the data against how complicated it is, to judge whether the results were suitable.

### Step 4: Finding the electricity mix in the NDCs

Under Article 4, paragraph 12 of the Paris Agreement, the nationally determined contributions that countries send in are kept in a public register run by the secretariat (UNFCCC, 2024). For most countries, we used the values they gave for the capacity they plan to install, for each country c and fuel f. Because the NDCs do not always say which technology will be used, we assumed that each country c will use the technology t that is most available for its NDC expansion.

Often, the NDCs say nothing about electricity supply or the electricity mix (the share of electricity that comes from each fuel and technology). They only give goals for installed capacity or for the share of renewable energy. This was the case for Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Kenya, Madagascar, Mauritius, Sierra Leone and Zambia. For all of these except Kenya, we treated the NDC as the same as our INVENTORY. For Kenya, we took the future electricity mix from a report by the Kenyan Ministry of Energy and Petroleum (reference 51).

To estimate electricity production in 2030, we assumed that the electricity mix from our record also holds for the NDCs. Using our record, we found the electricity mix for country c, fuel f and technology t for 2030, and calculated electricity production, E2030,c,f,t (MW), with Eq. (2).

### Step 5: Water withdrawal, water consumption and CO2 emissions from electricity, 2020–2030

In Step 5, we calculated the water withdrawal, water consumption and CO2 emissions linked to electricity production for each country from 2020 to 2030. For water withdrawal and consumption, we only counted the water used while a plant is running, and left out the water used to make the materials for the plant. We calculated freshwater consumption for each country n and energy source s, Watern,s (cubic metres per year, m³ per year), as in Eq. (7):

(7) Watern,s = En,s × Ws,o,c

Here, En,s is the electricity made by energy source s (MWh per year) in country n. Ws,o,c is the specific freshwater consumption of energy source s: how many cubic metres of fresh water each megawatt-hour uses, for operating feature o (the operating cycle and the equipment) in climate c (m³ per MWh). We calculated freshwater withdrawal and CO2 emissions in the same way, using the specific freshwater withdrawal of energy source s in climate c. For this, we followed the method of Gerbens-Leenes and colleagues (2024) and used CO2 emissions figures from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), 2024. We used different factors for each power plant, depending on its climate and type.

The water figures are based on these climate zones, taken from Kottek and colleagues (reference 64): Tropical Rainforest (Af), Tropical Monsoon (Am), Tropical Savannah (Aw), Arid Steppe Hot (BSh), Desert Hot (BWh), Humid subtropical (Cfa), Temperate Without dry Season (Cfb), hot-summer Mediterranean (Csa), warm-summer Mediterranean (Csb), Dry-winter humid subtropical (Cwa), Dry-winter subtropical highland (Cwb).

For hydropower, we calculated how much water each plant loses to evaporation, depending on the size of its reservoir, the climate or other equipment.

All the information and data are included in Supplementary Tables 4–6 in the Supplementary Information.

Next, we calculated freshwater consumption for each country n, Water,n (m³ per year), as in Eq. (8):

(8) Watern = Σ(s=1 to t) Watern,s

We calculated freshwater withdrawal and CO2 emissions for each country n in the same way.

#### How much of the renewable water in Africa's major river basins is needed for electricity, according to INVENTORY

We measured how the water needed for electricity compares with the renewable water available in Africa's major river basins. We defined renewable water availability as natural renewable water minus environmental flows (EFs), as in Eq. (9):

(9) renewable water availability = natural renewable water − EF

We took natural renewable water, mapped in fine detail (0.1 degrees, or 11.1 km at the equator), from Vanham and colleagues (reference 65). They used a computer model of how water moves through the land, called LISFLOOD (reference 66). The model works day by day for the years 1980 to 2018, and it gives natural water availability as the total of renewable water on the surface and underground. We used the map of river basins and smaller river areas from Hydrosheds (reference 67) to add up the natural renewable water in each grid square into each basin.

Environmental flows are the amount and timing of water that rivers and streams need to keep their living systems working. They keep the parts, processes and resilience of water ecosystems in place, along with the goods and services these ecosystems give people. They are needed to keep streams, rivers, wetlands, the land along riverbanks and estuaries healthy. Environmental flows also provide many other benefits from nature, which are directly linked to particular Sustainable Development Goals (references 27 and 68).

To measure environmental flows, we used the standard proposed by Richter and colleagues (reference 34), which sets environmental flows at 80% of the natural flow. The other 20% is seen as water that people can use, which in this paper we call renewable water availability. This standard is widely used in studies of water management (references 23, 30 and 69–72). It is backed by studies showing that changing river flows by up to 20% still supports native fish species, while changing them by more than this strongly affects the variety of life and how ecosystems are built and work (reference 73).

We did not carry out a full assessment of water stress, which would need the water needs of every group that uses water, such as farming (reference 31), towns and cities, mining and industry. The reason is that, for many of these groups, there are no detailed maps as detailed as our energy assessment.

### How sure we are

To allow for uncertainty about future power plants up to 2030 in INVENTORY, we allowed for delays before plants start working. Solar power plants and wind farms take a fairly short time to plan and build (reference 14), so we assumed a delay of one year (reference 74). The ACP, for example, reports that solar and wind projects are delayed by 13 months on average (reference 74). In Africa, the 120 MW Kairouan Solar Photovoltaic Project in Tunisia was first planned to start working in 2024 (reference 75), but this was pushed back to 2025 (reference 76).

For all other power plants, which take longer on average to plan and build (reference 14), we assumed a delay of two years. Fossil-fuelled thermal plants take almost 5 years to build on average (reference 14), so adding two years is an increase of 40%. One example is the Egbema gas-fired power station in Nigeria, which INVENTORY says will start working in 2024 (reference 77), but which was delayed to 2026 (reference 78). We also picked out planned nuclear power plants and large hydropower plants, because they take a long time to plan and build. If recent information suggested a real chance of a delay, we left them out. In this way, we calculated electricity production by 2030 for an INVENTORY analysis that includes large delays.

For our assessment of how much of the renewable water in Africa's major basins is needed for electricity, according to INVENTORY, we also allowed for uncertainty. We repeated the same analysis using a measure of environmental flows that matches the lowest flows recommended for rivers, called the monthly Q95: the flow that is exceeded 95% of the time in each month (references 30 and 60). This gives a range, from a high level of protection for environmental flows (the flows set by Richter and colleagues, reference 34) to a low level (Q95). The results are shown in Supplementary Fig. 2.

We also allowed for uncertainty in our forecasts of future electricity production up to 2030, which are based on past data (from 1990 to 2015, as well as on the 2020 record and its 2023 update). For this, we used three different regression methods as well as ARIMA.

We first submitted this paper in November 2024, and it was published in 2026. So we present our analysis up to 2023 as existing data, and all later years (2024–2030) as forecasts.
